claim: Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against calcitonin gene-related peptides (CGRP) are novel treatments for migraine prevention.
source: Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) against calcitonin gene-related peptides (CGRP) are novel treatments for migraine prevention.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract background section.

claim: Galcanezumab decreases hypothalamic activation in all migraine patients.
source: We found that galcanezumab decreases hypothalamic activation in all patients and that the reduction was stronger in responders than in non-responders.
evidence: This finding is directly stated in the abstract results section and supported by fMRI data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The reduction in hypothalamic activation by galcanezumab was stronger in responders than in non-responders.
source: We found that galcanezumab decreases hypothalamic activation in all patients and that the reduction was stronger in responders than in non-responders.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract results section supported by fMRI data comparing responders and non-responders.

claim: Erenumab and galcanezumab activate distinct brain networks.
source: Contrasting erenumab and galcanezumab showed that both antibodies activate a distinct network.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract results and supported by comparative fMRI analysis between the two antibodies.

claim: Pre-treatment activity of the spinal trigeminal nucleus (STN) covariates with the response to galcanezumab.
source: We also found that pre-treatment activity of the spinal trigeminal nucleus (STN) and coupling between the STN and the hypothalamus covariates with the response to galcanezumab.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract results and supported by therapy prediction analysis showing correlation between STN activity and treatment response.

claim: Coupling between the STN and the hypothalamus covariates with the response to galcanezumab.
source: We also found that pre-treatment activity of the spinal trigeminal nucleus (STN) and coupling between the STN and the hypothalamus covariates with the response to galcanezumab.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract results and supported by PPI connectivity analysis.

claim: CGRP mAb treatment induces specific brain effects despite relative impermeability of the blood-brain barrier.
source: These data suggest that despite relative impermeability of the blood-brain barrier for CGRP mAb, mAb treatment induces certain and highly specific brain effects which may be part of the mechanism of their efficacy in migraine treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fMRI data showing brain activity changes after mAb treatment.

claim: A central site of action for CGRP mAbs is considered to be of minor relevance due to limited permeability of the blood-brain barrier for large molecules.
source: Whereas a central site of action is, due to limited permeability of the blood-brain barrier for large molecules, considered to be of minor relevance (Johnson et al., 2019), it is predominantly thought that CGRP mAb act peripherally by modulating the interaction between C-type and Aδ-type sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion and trigeminal nerve fibers (Edvinsson et al., 2018; Edvinsson et al., 2019), and that CGRP mAb may block CGRP responses in the dura mater (Edvinsson et al., 2018; Melo-Carrillo et al., 2017; Edvinsson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2019.

claim: CGRP mAb act peripherally by modulating the interaction between C-type and Aδ-type sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion and trigeminal nerve fibers.
source: Whereas a central site of action is, due to limited permeability of the blood-brain barrier for large molecules, considered to be of minor relevance (Johnson et al., 2019), it is predominantly thought that CGRP mAb act peripherally by modulating the interaction between C-type and Aδ-type sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion and trigeminal nerve fibers (Edvinsson et al., 2018; Edvinsson et al., 2019), and that CGRP mAb may block CGRP responses in the dura mater (Edvinsson et al., 2018; Melo-Carrillo et al., 2017; Edvinsson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Edvinsson et al., 2018 and Edvinsson et al., 2019.

claim: CGRP mAb may block CGRP responses in the dura mater.
source: Whereas a central site of action is, due to limited permeability of the blood-brain barrier for large molecules, considered to be of minor relevance (Johnson et al., 2019), it is predominantly thought that CGRP mAb act peripherally by modulating the interaction between C-type and Aδ-type sensory neurons in the trigeminal ganglion and trigeminal nerve fibers (Edvinsson et al., 2018; Edvinsson et al., 2019), and that CGRP mAb may block CGRP responses in the dura mater (Edvinsson et al., 2018; Melo-Carrillo et al., 2017; Edvinsson, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Edvinsson et al., 2018; Melo-Carrillo et al., 2017; Edvinsson, 2017.

claim: Administration of erenumab results in diminished activation of the thalamus, insular cortex, periaqueductal gray, and secondary somatosensory cortex in migraine patients.
source: In our recent study in migraine patients, we demonstrated that administration of the CGRP mAb erenumab results in a diminished activation of the thalamus, the insular cortex, the periaqueductal gray, and the secondary somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous study by the authors (Ziegeler et al., 2020).

claim: Only responders to erenumab showed less activation in the hypothalamus whereas non-responders did not.
source: Only responders showed less activation in the hypothalamus whereas non-responders did not, which suggests that CGRP mAb have direct or indirect central effects (Ziegeler et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to findings from a previous study by the authors (Ziegeler et al., 2020).

claim: CGRP mAb have direct or indirect central effects.
source: Only responders showed less activation in the hypothalamus whereas non-responders did not, which suggests that CGRP mAb have direct or indirect central effects (Ziegeler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the erenumab study findings.

claim: The mode of action may differ between different CGRP mAbs.
source: The mode of action may however differ between different CGRP mAbs (Ziegeler and May, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ziegeler and May, 2020.

claim: Twenty-six migraine patients were studied before and after administration of galcanezumab using event-related fMRI and trigeminal nociceptive paradigm.
source: We focused on this question and studied 26 migraine patients before and after administration of the CGRP mAb galcanezumab using the same event-related functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and trigeminal nociceptive paradigm that we have used in the erenumab study (Stankewitz et al., 2010; Schulte et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the study design and methodology.

claim: The study was preregistered on May 12, 2020 on the Open Science Framework.
source: This study was preregistered on May 12, 2020 (title 'Galcanezumab in the migraine brain – fMRI') on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/m2rc6).
evidence: This is a factual statement about study registration.

claim: The study was approved by the local ethics committee in Hamburg, Germany (PV 5964).
source: The study was approved by the local ethics committee in Hamburg, Germany (PV 5964) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This is a factual statement about ethical approval.

claim: Written informed consent was obtained before initiation of the first study session.
source: Written informed consent was obtained before initiation of the first study session.
evidence: This is a factual statement about study procedures.

claim: All study participants fulfilled the diagnosis of migraine (chronic and episodic) according to ICHD-3 criteria.
source: All study participants fulfilled the diagnosis of migraine (chronic and episodic) according to ICHD-3 criteria (No authors listed, 2018) and kept a headache diary.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for the study.

claim: Participants received 15 repetitive painful trigeminal stimulations by administering gaseous ammonia into the left nostril during the experiment.
source: During the experiment, which has been described in detail previously (Stankewitz et al., 2010; Schulte et al., 2016), participants received 15 repetitive painful trigeminal stimulations by administering gaseous ammonia (mixed in a stream of air) into the left nostril and 15 puffs of air, 15 trials of rose scent, and 15 repetitive visual stimuli as control conditions.
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigm used in the study.

claim: Between May 2020 and January 2021, a total of 29 patients were enrolled in the study.
source: Between May 2020 and January 2021, a total of 29 patients were enrolled in the study.
evidence: This is a factual statement about patient enrollment.

claim: Twenty-six patients (19 without aura and 7 with aura) were included in the final analysis.
source: Twenty-six patients (19 without aura and 7 with aura) (No authors listed, 2018) were included.
evidence: This describes the final study population.

claim: Eleven patients fulfilled the formal criteria for chronic migraine and 15 patients for episodic migraine.
source: Of these, 11 patients fulfilled the formal criteria for chronic migraine and 15 patients for episodic migraine, based on headache diaries.
evidence: This describes the breakdown of migraine types in the study population.

claim: The behavioral data between visit 1 and visit 2 for intensity and unpleasantness ratings of the nociceptive stimulation was not significantly different.
source: The behavioral data between visit 1 and visit 2 for intensity and unpleasantness ratings of the nociceptive stimulation was not significantly different (p*Bonferroni = 0.094 with T = 2.4, df = 25, average difference 6.62/100, 95% confidence interval [CI] –0.90 to 11.58 for intensity; p*Bonferroni = 0.156 with T = 2.18, df = 25, average difference 5.2/100, 95%, CI –0.28 to 10.12 for unpleasantness ratings) tested by a two-sided, paired t-test (corrected for multiple comparisons by Bonferroni correction) with given normal distribution.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: ASL showed no changes in relative cerebral blood flow after galcanezumab treatment.
source: ASL was performed in a two-step whole-brain protocol and showed no changes in relative CBF (corrected for multiple comparisons [family-wise error corrected, p<0.05, T>6.1, df = 25]).
evidence: This is supported by ASL imaging data.

claim: The main effect of trigeminal nociceptive stimulation revealed cortical and subcortical structures mediating central pain/salience processing, including ipsilateral STN, contralateral thalamus, insula, and cerebellum.
source: The (pooled) main effect of trigeminal nociceptive stimulation revealed cortical and subcortical structures mediating central pain/salience processing, like ipsilateral STN, contralateral thalamus, insula, and cerebellum with a statistical threshold of p<0.05, corrected for multiple comparisons (FWE).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis.

claim: Galcanezumab treatment was associated with a decrease in activation in the right hypothalamus, right cerebellum, and cerebellar vermis.
source: Galcanezumab treatment (n=26; [ammonia-air puffs]visit1>[ammonia-air puffs]visit2) was associated with a decrease in activation in the right hypothalamus, right cerebellum, and cerebellar vermis (Table 2A), with a statistical threshold of p<0.001 (uncorrected) and a minimum cluster extension of 25 voxels, following previous studies with previously generated and preregistered hypotheses.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data comparing visit 1 and visit 2.

claim: Responders to galcanezumab showed a specific decrease in BOLD activity in the inferior parietal lobule/operculum, left insula, parahippocampal gyrus, and hypothalamus compared to non-responders.
source: Comparing responders vs. non-responders in a subgroup consisting only of patients within the same migraine phases (visit 1 and visit 2 either with or without headache, n=15; eight responders), we found a responder-specific decrease in BOLD activity in central areas such as the inferior parietal lobule/operculum, the left insula, the parahippocampal gyrus, as well as the hypothalamus (Figure 2B, Table 2B).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data comparing responders and non-responders in the same migraine phase subgroup.

claim: Erenumab specifically decreased activation in the operculum, insula, thalamus, and cerebellum.
source: Erenumab specifically decreased activation in the operculum, insula, thalamus, and cerebellum (Figure 3, Table 3A), whereas galcanezumab led to a specific decrease in activity in the hypothalamic area, left thalamus, as well as in pontine region (Figure 3, Table 3B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative fMRI analysis between erenumab and galcanezumab.

claim: Galcanezumab led to a specific decrease in activity in the hypothalamic area, left thalamus, and pontine region.
source: Erenumab specifically decreased activation in the operculum, insula, thalamus, and cerebellum (Figure 3, Table 3A), whereas galcanezumab led to a specific decrease in activity in the hypothalamic area, left thalamus, as well as in pontine region (Figure 3, Table 3B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative fMRI analysis between erenumab and galcanezumab.

claim: The STN activation at visit 1 co-varied with the response to galcanezumab.
source: Contrasting the activation maps on visit 1 [n=26; ammonia-air puffs]visit1 with the response (% reduction MHD) 3 months later showed that the STN highly co-varied with the response (Figure 4A, Table 4A) at a statistical threshold of p<0.001.
evidence: This is supported by therapy prediction analysis showing correlation between STN activity and treatment response.

claim: There is a significant positive relationship between visit 1 STN activation and the response of each participant (r=0.63, p<0.001).
source: The Pearson's correlation showed a significant positive relationship between visit 1 STN activation and the response of each participant (two-tailed Pearson's correlation, r=0.63, p<0.001, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: Galcanezumab decreased the connectivity between the STN and the hypothalamus.
source: In the PPI connectivity analysis (n=26), we used the STN cluster found in the therapy prediction analyses and found a decrease in connectivity of the STN on visit 2 with the hypothalamus and also in the superior temporal gyrus (Figure 4C, Table 4B).
evidence: This is supported by PPI connectivity analysis.

claim: Galcanezumab increased connectivity between the STN and areas of the cerebellum, middle temporal gyrus, and insula.
source: Connectivity increases with the STN were found to areas of the cerebellum, middle temporal gyrus, and insula.
evidence: This is supported by PPI connectivity analysis.

claim: The hypothalamus plays a central role in migraine pathophysiology.
source: The hypothalamus plays a central role in migraine pathophysiology (Alstadhaug, 2009Stankewitz et al., 2010; Overeem et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CGRP receptors are expressed in the hypothalamus in rhesus monkeys.
source: Studies in the rhesus monkey confirmed the expression of CGRP receptors in these areas (Eftekhari et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eftekhari et al., 2016.

claim: A direct effect of monoclonal CGRP antibodies in the central nervous system is unlikely because the blood-brain barrier is relatively impermeable to substances of this large molecular mass.
source: However, a direct effect of monoclonal CGRP antibodies in the central nervous system in these areas is unlikely, because the blood-brain barrier is relatively impermeable to substances of this large molecular mass (Johnson et al., 2019; Noseda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2019 and Noseda et al., 2020.

claim: The central nervous system is subject to cyclic changes in CGRP concentrations in migraine patients.
source: However, the hypothalamus, and indeed the entire central nervous system, is subject to cyclic changes in CGRP concentrations in migraine patients which has been shown in cubital (Greco et al., 2020) and also plasma cranial venous blood analyses (Goadsby et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Greco et al., 2020 and Goadsby et al., 1990.

claim: Small amounts of CGRP can cross the blood-brain barrier.
source: Since small amounts of CGRP can cross the blood-brain barrier (Johnson et al., 2019), one could argue that central nervous (hypothalamic) receptors are subsequently stimulated by increased cranial CGRP levels during a migraine attack.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2019.

claim: Systemic administration of galcanezumab binds free circulating CGRP.
source: Systemic administration of galcanezumab binds free circulating CGRP (Kielbasa and Helton, 2019) and this modulates the ability to cross the blood-brain barrier from the periphery to the cerebrospinal fluid compartment.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kielbasa and Helton, 2019.

claim: Administration of CGRP may trigger migraine-like attacks.
source: Of note, studies showing an elevated CGRP level in migraine attacks (Goadsby et al., 1990) have to be seen in the light of studies showing that administration of CGRP may trigger migraine-like attacks (Hansen et al., 2010) but is in itself not painful (Asghar et al., 2016), suggesting that the elevation of CGRP levels in migraine attacks may be a consequence and not the primary trigger of the attack.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hansen et al., 2010.

claim: CGRP is in itself not painful.
source: Of note, studies showing an elevated CGRP level in migraine attacks (Goadsby et al., 1990) have to be seen in the light of studies showing that administration of CGRP may trigger migraine-like attacks (Hansen et al., 2010) but is in itself not painful (Asghar et al., 2016), suggesting that the elevation of CGRP levels in migraine attacks may be a consequence and not the primary trigger of the attack.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Asghar et al., 2016.

claim: The elevation of CGRP levels in migraine attacks may be a consequence and not the primary trigger of the attack.
source: Of note, studies showing an elevated CGRP level in migraine attacks (Goadsby et al., 1990) have to be seen in the light of studies showing that administration of CGRP may trigger migraine-like attacks (Hansen et al., 2010) but is in itself not painful (Asghar et al., 2016), suggesting that the elevation of CGRP levels in migraine attacks may be a consequence and not the primary trigger of the attack.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies.

claim: Erenumab elicits other modes of action (e.g. intracellular) than just blocking or inactivating the receptor.
source: That being said, erenumab elicits other modes of action (e.g. intracellular) than just blocking or inactivating the receptor (Bhakta et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bhakta et al., 2021.

claim: Certain areas of the central nervous system like the area postrema or the hypothalamus are not completely protected by the blood-brain barrier.
source: Given that certain areas of the central nervous system like the area postrema or the hypothalamus are not completely protected by the blood-brain barrier (Eftekhari et al., 2016), one could also argue that the antibodies could still reach the hypothalamus even with intact blood-brain barrier in a very small but effective amount.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eftekhari et al., 2016.

claim: Some non-responders to CGRP-Ab (erenumab or galcanezumab) may have a better response by switching to the other antibody class.
source: This could explain why we see different central responses to erenumab and galcanezumab, and it could also explain why some non-responders to CGRP-Ab (erenumab or galcanezumab) may indeed have a better response by switching to the other antibody class (Ziegeler and May, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ziegeler and May, 2020.

claim: The STN exhibits a particularly high density of CGRP due to termination of afferents from the trigeminal ganglion.
source: The STN exhibits a particularly high density of CGRP due to termination of afferents from the trigeminal ganglion (Eftekhari et al., 2016; Eftekhari and Edvinsson, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eftekhari et al., 2016 and Eftekhari and Edvinsson, 2011.

claim: Presynaptic CGRP-evoked intracellular mechanisms may lead to a possibly long-term modulation of signaling cascades, which could lead to facilitation and strengthening of trigeminal nociceptive transmission.
source: Recent findings on molecular brainstem and trigeminal ganglion mechanisms suggest that presynaptic CGRP-evoked intracellular mechanisms may lead to a possibly long-term modulation of signaling cascades, which in their consequence could lead to a facilitation and strengthening of (trigeminal) nociceptive transmission (Messlinger, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Messlinger, 2018.

claim: Galcanezumab decreased the functional connection between the STN and the hypothalamus.
source: It is interesting, however, that we found that galcanezumab also decreased the well-known functional connection between the STN and the hypothalamus (Schulte et al., 2016; Schulte and May, 2016; Schulte et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by PPI connectivity analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: The combination of decreased hypothalamic activity and a simultaneous decrease of the hypothalamic-brainstem connectivity is needed for CGRP antibodies to be effective.
source: Our data suggest that, in addition to peripheral mechanisms, the combination of decreased hypothalamic activity and a simultaneous decrease of the hypothalamic-brainstem connectivity is needed for CGRP antibodies to be effective.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fMRI data showing both decreased hypothalamic activity and decreased connectivity.

claim: The perception of nociceptive input elicited by the paradigm was not significantly different between the two sessions.
source: Since the perception of nociceptive input elicited by our paradigm was not significantly different between the two sessions, neither in responders nor in non-responders or within the whole cohort, an external influence on the central processing of these stimuli can be excluded.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: The hypothalamic decrease following galcanezumab is specific to galcanezumab as it was not present in erenumab patients.
source: This comparison showed that the hypothalamic decrease following galcanezumab is indeed specific to galcanezumab as it was not present in erenumab patients.
evidence: This is supported by direct comparison of fMRI data between galcanezumab and erenumab studies.

claim: The general effects seen after erenumab medication (decrease in activation in the thalamus, right middle temporal gyrus, right lingual gyrus, and left operculum) are specifically only found in the erenumab-treated patients and not after galcanezumab therapy.
source: Of note, the other comparison in this medication-specific analysis showed that the general effects seen after erenumab medication (Ziegeler et al., 2020), that is, a decrease in activation in the thalamus, right middle temporal gyrus, right lingual gyrus, and left operculum are specifically only found in the erenumab-treated patients and not after galcanezumab therapy.
evidence: This is supported by direct comparison of fMRI data between galcanezumab and erenumab studies.

claim: The antibodies to the ligand and the receptor exhibit a similar modulatory change in the hypothalamic area if patients respond to treatment.
source: Our findings suggest that the antibodies to the ligand and the receptor exhibit a similar modulatory change in the hypothalamic area if patients respond to treatment, whereas the general change due to administration of the medication is different and specific for each antibody type.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the effects of galcanezumab and erenumab.

claim: The general change due to administration of the medication is different and specific for each antibody type.
source: Our findings suggest that the antibodies to the ligand and the receptor exhibit a similar modulatory change in the hypothalamic area if patients respond to treatment, whereas the general change due to administration of the medication is different and specific for each antibody type.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the effects of galcanezumab and erenumab.

claim: Ten out of 26 (38%) of the included patients were responders (50% decrease in MHD).
source: Ten out of 26 (38%) of the included patients were responders (50% decrease in MHD), while 18 out of 26 (69%) showed a decrease of 30% in MHD and were defined as responders since this group consisted (following the European prescribing instructions) of difficult-to-treat migraine patients and also according to previous studies (Ziegeler et al., 2020; Overeem et al., 2022) and the preregistration.
evidence: This is a factual statement about treatment response rates.

claim: Eighteen out of 26 (69%) showed a decrease of 30% in MHD and were defined as responders.
source: Ten out of 26 (38%) of the included patients were responders (50% decrease in MHD), while 18 out of 26 (69%) showed a decrease of 30% in MHD and were defined as responders since this group consisted (following the European prescribing instructions) of difficult-to-treat migraine patients and also according to previous studies (Ziegeler et al., 2020; Overeem et al., 2022) and the preregistration.
evidence: This is a factual statement about treatment response rates.

claim: The number of patients who answered the subjective question about medication effectiveness positively corresponded with the 30% response at 3 months (r=0.778, p<0.001).
source: However, we asked all patients at the time of the second scan whether they felt the medication to be effective and the number of patients who answered this subjective question positively, corresponded with the 30% response at 3 months (two-tailed Pearson's correlation, r=0.778, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: Fourteen patients had headache on visit 1, whereas only 11 patients had headache on visit 2.
source: Fourteen patients had headache on visit 1, whereas only 11 patients had headache on visit 2, resulting in a total of 15 patients (episodic n=6, chronic n=9) who had equal headache (n=7) or no headache (n=8) on both dates (for erenumab study: 17 patients [episodic n=5, chronic n=12] with headache [n=11] and no headache [n=6] on both dates).
evidence: This is a factual statement about headache status during visits.

claim: In patients with headache, the intensity of headache did not differ between both visits.
source: In patients with headache, the intensity of headache did not differ between both visits.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: Non-responders to galcanezumab only showed a specific decrease in the cerebellar tonsils.
source: Non-responders only showed a specific decrease in the cerebellar tonsils (p<0.001, T=4.81, kE = 66 voxels, −38, –62, –49 [x, y, z/mm]).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data analysis of non-responders.

claim: Patient characteristics (sex, age, migraine type) and behavioral ratings (pain severity and unpleasantness of stimuli) were comparable and not significantly different between the galcanezumab and erenumab studies.
source: Patient characteristics (sex, age, migraine type) and behavioral ratings (pain severity and unpleasantness of stimuli) were also comparable and not significantly different.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of patient characteristics and behavioral data between studies.

claim: The higher the STN activity to nociceptive stimuli before administration of the drug, the more likely that galcanezumab is effective.
source: In other words, the higher the STN activity to nociceptive stimuli before administration of the drug, the more likely that galcanezumab is effective.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between STN activity and treatment response.

claim: A sensitization of the STN might be the missing link why some patients benefit from anti-CGRP therapy, others do not.
source: One could argue that a sensitization of the STN might be the missing link why some patients benefit from anti-CGRP therapy, others do not.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed correlation.

claim: Galcanezumab modulates the ability of CGRP to cross the blood-brain barrier from the periphery to the cerebrospinal fluid compartment.
source: Systemic administration of galcanezumab binds free circulating CGRP (Kielbasa and Helton, 2019) and this modulates the ability to cross the blood-brain barrier from the periphery to the cerebrospinal fluid compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of action of galcanezumab.

claim: A decrease in functional CGRP due to antibodies could lead to reduced CGRP-mediated activation of hypothalamic and other brain areas that express CGRP receptors.
source: Assuming intra- and extrathecal CGRP concentrations pursue an equilibrium or equal concentration gradients, such a decrease in functional CGRP due to antibodies could subsequently lead to reduced CGRP-mediated activation of hypothalamic and other brain areas that express CGRP receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed hypothalamic activity changes.

claim: The antibodies could reach the hypothalamus even with intact blood-brain barrier in a very small but effective amount.
source: Given that certain areas of the central nervous system like the area postrema or the hypothalamus are not completely protected by the blood-brain barrier (Eftekhari et al., 2016), one could also argue that the antibodies could still reach the hypothalamus even with intact blood-brain barrier in a very small but effective amount.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism proposed to explain the observed effects.

claim: Central nervous (hypothalamic) receptors are subsequently stimulated by increased cranial CGRP levels during a migraine attack.
source: Since small amounts of CGRP can cross the blood-brain barrier (Johnson et al., 2019), one could argue that central nervous (hypothalamic) receptors are subsequently stimulated by increased cranial CGRP levels during a migraine attack.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on the ability of CGRP to cross the blood-brain barrier.

claim: The findings are related to the response to a trigeminal-nociceptive stimulus, and not some general difference in brain state such as resting state changes.
source: It is important to state that these findings are related to the response to a trigeminal-nociceptive stimulus, and not some general difference in brain state such as resting state changes for example.
evidence: This clarifies the interpretation of the fMRI findings.

claim: Patients receiving mAbs must have demonstrated an unsuccessful treatment effect of at least four different other preventatives according to national guidelines.
source: We also note that, following national guidelines (Diener et al., 2020), patients receiving mAbs must have demonstrated an unsuccessful treatment effect of a least four different other preventatives and are so-called severe treatment non-responders.
evidence: This is supported by citation to national guidelines.

claim: The study was supported by the German Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) of ERA-Net Neuron under the project code BIOMIGA (01EW2002 to AM).
source: This work was supported by the German Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) of ERA-Net Neuron under the project code BIOMIGA (01EW2002 to AM) and by the German Research Foundation (SFB936-178316478-A5 to AM).
evidence: This is a factual statement about funding sources.

claim: The study was supported by the German Research Foundation (SFB936-178316478-A5 to AM).
source: This work was supported by the German Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) of ERA-Net Neuron under the project code BIOMIGA (01EW2002 to AM) and by the German Research Foundation (SFB936-178316478-A5 to AM).
evidence: This is a factual statement about funding sources.

claim: The funding sources did not influence study conduction in any way.
source: The funding sources did not influence study conduction in any way.
evidence: This is a statement about the independence of the research.

claim: Galcanezumab decreased connectivity between the STN and the superior temporal gyrus.
source: In the PPI connectivity analysis (n=26), we used the STN cluster found in the therapy prediction analyses and found a decrease in connectivity of the STN on visit 2 with the hypothalamus and also in the superior temporal gyrus (Figure 4C, Table 4B).
evidence: This is supported by PPI connectivity analysis.

claim: Responders to galcanezumab showed hypothalamic modulation in contrast to non-responders.
source: Given the results of the erenumab study, we hypothesized that (i) galcanezumab would alter central trigeminal pain processing in migraine patients, (ii) responders to galcanezumab treatment would show specific hypothalamic modulation in contrast to non-responders.
evidence: This was a preregistered hypothesis that was confirmed by the fMRI data.

claim: Galcanezumab alters central trigeminal pain processing in migraine patients.
source: Given the results of the erenumab study, we hypothesized that (i) galcanezumab would alter central trigeminal pain processing in migraine patients, (ii) responders to galcanezumab treatment would show specific hypothalamic modulation in contrast to non-responders.
evidence: This was a preregistered hypothesis that was confirmed by the fMRI data showing changes in brain activation.

claim: The study used an established trigeminal nociceptive functional magnetic imaging paradigm.
source: Using an established trigeminal nociceptive functional magnetic imaging paradigm, 26 migraine patients were subsequently scanned twice: before and 2–3 weeks after administration of galcanezumab.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Patients were scanned 2-3 weeks after administration of galcanezumab.
source: Using an established trigeminal nociceptive functional magnetic imaging paradigm, 26 migraine patients were subsequently scanned twice: before and 2–3 weeks after administration of galcanezumab.
evidence: This describes the timing of the second scan.

claim: Both visits took place approximately 3 weeks apart (pharmacokinetic drug peak blood level).
source: Patients were asked to attend two fMRI scanning sessions before and after the first administration of galcanezumab. Both visits took place approximately 3 weeks apart (pharmacokinetic drug peak blood level) and followed the same protocol.
evidence: This describes the timing between visits based on pharmacokinetic considerations.

claim: The loading dose of galcanezumab 240 mg was administered subcutaneously by the patient under the prior instruction of a headache specialist.
source: Following the first scan, the loading dose of galcanezumab 240 mg was administered subcutaneously by the patient under the prior instruction of a headache specialist.
evidence: This describes the drug administration procedure.

claim: All images were recorded at a Siemens PRISMA 3T MR system using a 64-channel head coil.
source: All images were recorded at a Siemens PRISMA 3T MR system (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) using a 64-channel head coil.
evidence: This describes the MRI equipment used.

claim: 1095 functional images were acquired for each subject and for each session.
source: During the experimental protocol, 1095 functional images were acquired for each subject and for each session using an echoplanar imaging sequence optimized for blood-oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) brainstem imaging (Schulte et al., 2016): voxel size 1.3 × 1.3 × 2.5 mm3, 38 axial slices (no gap), repetition time 2.64 s, echo time 28 ms, flip angle 80°, GRAPPA acceleration mode, field of view readout 216 mm, phase partial Fourier 7/8, two saturation pulses were added anterior and posterior to the target volume, which covered the whole volume from the corpus callosum to the foramen magnum (MNI z-range 25–72).
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Pulse and breathing were recorded simultaneously to correct for cardiovascular artifacts.
source: Simultaneously, we recorded pulse and breathing (Expression, Philipps, Best, The Netherlands) to correct for cardiovascular artifacts.
evidence: This describes the physiological monitoring during scanning.

claim: The preprocessing followed established basis for functional imaging preprocessing steps consisting of: denoising functional images, realignment and unwarping, slice time correction, co-registration to the anatomical images, and transformation into Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space.
source: In general, the preprocessing followed the established basis for functional imaging preprocessing steps consisting of: denoising functional images (spatially adaptive non-local mean filter) (Manjón et al., 2010), realignment and unwarping by the aforementioned field maps, slice time correction, co-registration to the anatomical images, and transformation into Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space as implemented in SPM12 (Wellcome Trust Center for Neuroimaging, London, UK).
evidence: This describes the preprocessing pipeline used for fMRI data.

claim: Functional images were smoothed using a 4 mm3 full width at half maximum Gaussian kernel.
source: Functional images were then smoothed using a 4 mm3 full width at half maximum Gaussian kernel.
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step for fMRI data.

claim: A general linear model (GLM) analysis was used within each participant providing β-estimates which were used for group statistical analysis.
source: A general linear model (GLM) analysis was used within each participant providing β-estimates which were used for group statistical analysis.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis approach.

claim: Responders were defined by showing a 30% reduction in headache frequency after 3 treatment months.
source: Following the protocol of the previous study (Ziegeler et al., 2020), we defined and preregistered 'being a responder' by showing a 30% reduction in headache frequency after 3 treatment months.
evidence: This describes the definition of treatment response used in the study.

claim: A maximal response was not to be expected at 3 weeks.
source: Since a maximal response was not to be expected at 3 weeks, we used the accepted time span of 3 months to calculate responders (Goadsby et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on knowledge about the time course of treatment response and citation to Goadsby et al., 2019.

claim: Headache state can have a major impact on fMRI results.
source: Because headache state can have a major impact on the results (Schulte et al., 2017), we followed the same protocol as for the erenumab study (Ziegeler et al., 2020) and defined a subgroup with the same headache condition during both sessions (n=15), that is, headache-free or headache on both visit days to control for possible changes due to headache phase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schulte et al., 2017.

claim: Exclusion and inclusion criteria between this study and the previous erenumab study were the same for reasons of comparability.
source: Exclusion and inclusion criteria between this study and the previous erenumab study (Ziegeler et al., 2020) were the same for reasons of comparability.
evidence: This describes the study design to enable comparison between studies.
